title: Frame a Partition Wall
summary: Build a straight, plumb {{a.len}} ft non-load-bearing 2x4 wall{{a.door==='yes'?' with a door opening':''}}, fastened to the floor and ceiling and ready for drywall.
safety: Wear safety glasses with saws and nailers. Check for wires, pipes and ducts before nailing into floors and ceilings. Use a helper to tilt walls up. In attics, step only on framing.
pro: you're changing or removing an existing wall, the ceiling sags, the wall needs wiring or plumbing, or the room becomes a bedroom. Most areas require a permit for new walls: check local code.

steps.t: Check permits and what the wall is for
steps.idea: A new wall usually needs a permit, and a new bedroom has extra rules.
steps.stop: Call your building department before you start. Most areas require a permit for new walls. If the wall makes a new bedroom, it will need an egress window, smoke alarm and outlets: check local code.
steps.b:
1. Call or visit your local building department's website. Ask: "Do I need a permit for a non-load-bearing interior wall?"
  2. Tell them if the room becomes a bedroom. Bedrooms need an escape window of a minimum size, a smoke alarm and usually a CO alarm.
  3. Check where heat and cooling registers and the thermostat end up. Each room needs heat, and a closed room may need a return air path.
  4. New walls often need outlets by code. Plan for an electrician if so.
  5. Sketch the wall on paper with measurements to the existing walls.
faq: Will my wall be load-bearing?
No, a new partition carries no load as long as you don't jack it tight against the ceiling. Never remove or change an existing wall without an engineer or a pro.

steps.t: Find the ceiling joists and which way they run
steps.idea: The top plate must fasten into solid wood, so you need to know where the joists are.
steps.b:
1. Run a stud finder across the ceiling where the wall will go. Mark each joist.
  2. Marks in a row across the wall line, every 16" or 24"? Joists run perpendicular to your wall.
  3. No joist crosses your line? They run parallel. Find the nearest one on each side.
  4. Check from the attic if you can: look at the joists or trusses (triangle-shaped frames) directly.
  5. Set the "joists" and "above" answers on the Start tab.
faq: How do I know if I have trusses?
In the attic, trusses look like triangles of 2x4s joined by metal plates. Joists are single boards running wall to wall, with rafters above.

steps.t: Add blocking between parallel joists
steps.idea: Blocks between the joists give the top plate something to fasten to.
steps.b:
1. If you can, move the wall a few inches so it lands right under a joist. Then you can skip blocking.
  2. From the attic: measure between the joists (usually 14-1/2" for 16" spacing, 22-1/2" for 24").
  3. Cut {{c.blocks}} blocks from 2x4 or 2x6 to that length.
  4. Set them across the joists right above the wall line, every 24", resting on the ceiling drywall's back.
  5. Fasten each end with two 16d nails or 3" screws through the joist into the block.
  6. No attic access (floor above)? Cut a strip of ceiling drywall along the line, install blocks from below, and patch later.
steps.stop: Attics can be hot and have live wires and loose insulation. Step only on joists, never between them. Wear a mask in insulation.

steps.t: Snap the wall line on the floor
steps.idea: Two straight lines on the floor show exactly where the bottom plate goes.
steps.b:
1. Measure from the existing wall to the new wall's position at both ends. Mark both spots.
  2. Check square with the 3-4-5 method (picture): adjust until the 5 ft diagonal is exact.
  3. Snap a chalk line through the marks: this is one face of the wall.
  4. Snap a second line 3-1/2" over: the other face.
  5. Mark the door opening on the floor if you have one.
faq: The floor has carpet.
Cut it back along the wall line, or fasten through it into the subfloor. Most pros pull the carpet and pad back so the plate sits on the subfloor.

steps.t: Plumb the line up to the ceiling
steps.idea: The top plate must sit straight above the bottom plate, or the wall leans.
steps.b:
1. Set the laser on the floor line at one end. Turn it on and mark the dot on the ceiling.
  2. No laser: hang a plumb bob from the ceiling and move the string until the tip is over the line. Mark where the string meets the ceiling.
  3. Do the same at the other end.
  4. Snap a chalk line between the two ceiling marks.
  5. Check that it hits the joists or blocking you marked.

steps.t: Choose straight lumber
steps.idea: Straight studs make a flat wall. Crooked ones show as waves in the drywall.
steps.b:
1. At the store, sight down each board from one end. Reject twisted or badly bowed ones.
  2. Buy {{c.studs}} studs ({{c.buyStud}}) and the plate lumber in the list.
  3. At home, stack them flat, off the floor, for a day or two to adjust to the room.
  4. Before using each stud, find the crown (the slight hump) and mark it with an arrow.

steps.t: Cut the plates and mark the stud layout
steps.idea: Marking top and bottom plates together puts every stud perfectly straight up and down.
steps.b:
1. Cut the plates to the wall length: {{frac(a.len*12)}}. If one board isn't long enough, the joint must land on the center of a stud.
  2. Lay the {{a.floor==='concrete'?'treated bottom plate':'bottom plate'}} and top plate side by side, ends even, and clamp or tack them.
  3. Hook your tape on the end that starts the layout. Mark 15-1/4", then every 16": 31-1/4", 47-1/4" and so on.
  4. Use a square to draw each line across both plates. Put an X on the far side of each line: that's where the stud goes.
  5. Mark a stud flush at each end of the plates.
faq: Why 15-1/4" and not 16"?
So the 16" line falls in the middle of a stud. Drywall sheets are 48" wide; their edges then land on stud centers.

steps.t: Mark the door opening
steps.idea: The door opening replaces the regular studs in that spot with a king, jack and header on each side.
steps.b:
1. Find the opening's center on the plates.
  2. Mark half the rough opening ({{frac(c.ro/2)}}) each side of center. These lines are the inside faces of the jacks.
  3. Mark a jack (J) 1-1/2" outside each line, then a king (K) 1-1/2" beyond.
  4. Cross out regular layout marks that fall inside the opening; they become cripples above the header (C).
  5. Keep at least a full stud width between a king and the nearest layout stud, or just use the king as that stud.
faq: What size door?
Buy the door first. Rough opening width is the door width plus 2": {{a.doorW}}" door = {{c.ro}}". Check its instructions for both numbers.

steps.t: Cut the studs
steps.idea: All full-height studs are the same length, so cut one, check it, then copy it.
steps.b:
1. Measure the ceiling height at several spots along the line. Use the lowest.
  2. {{a.method==='tilt'?'Stud length for a tilt-up wall: '+frac(c.studLen)+' (wall '+frac(c.wallH)+' tall, about 1/2" short of the ceiling).':'Stick framing: cut each stud to fit between the installed plates, about '+frac(c.studLen)+'. Measure at each stud.'}}
  3. Cut one stud, test it, then use it as a pattern for the rest.
    4. {{a.door==='yes'?'
  4. Jacks: '+frac(c.jack)+' (2). Header (flat 2x4): '+frac(c.ro+3)+'. Cripples: '+frac(c.crip)+'.
    5. ':''}}
  5. Make every cut square: hold the saw base flat and follow a line drawn with the speed square.

steps.t: Nail the wall together on the floor
steps.idea: It's much easier to nail through the plates into the stud ends with the wall lying flat.
steps.b:
1. Lay the plates on edge, about a stud length apart, on the floor near the wall line.
  2. Set each stud on its X, crowns all facing the same way (up).
  3. Drive two 16d nails (or 3" screws) through the plate into each stud end.
  4. Keep the stud edges flush with the plate edges. Stand on the stud to hold it.
  5. {{a.topPlate==='double'?'Nail the second top plate on top of the first, staggering its joints at least 24" from the first plate\'s joints.':'Single top plate: done.'}}

steps.t: Frame the door opening
steps.idea: The jacks hold the header; the kings hold everything to the plates.
steps.b:
1. Nail the kings through the plates like any stud.
  2. Nail a jack to the inside face of each king: 16d nails every 16", staggered.
  3. Set the flat header on top of both jacks. Nail through the kings into its ends.
  4. Nail the cripples between the header and the top plate on the layout marks.
  5. Measure the opening: width {{c.ro}}", height {{frac(a.roH)}}. Fix it now if it's off.
faq: Is a flat 2x4 header OK?
On a non-bearing wall, many areas accept a single flat 2x or a doubled 2x4 header. Ask your inspector.

steps.t: Tilt the wall up
steps.idea: With a helper, swing the wall up onto its lines.
steps.stop: Get a helper. A wall section is heavy and awkward, and can fall over until it is fastened.
steps.b:
1. Slide the wall so the bottom plate sits just beside its floor line.
  2. Lift the top plate end together, walking your hands down the studs.
  3. If it jams on the ceiling, stop: tap the bottom out and tilt more slowly, or trim the studs.
  4. Tap the bottom plate onto its chalk lines with a hammer and a scrap block.
  5. Have your helper hold it while you fasten the bottom plate (next step).

steps.t: Fasten the plates first
steps.idea: In stick framing, the plates go up first and the studs fit between them.
steps.b:
1. Fasten the bottom plate on its floor lines (next step explains the fasteners).
  2. Hold the top plate on its ceiling line and fasten it to each joist or block.
  3. Shim any gap above the plate before fastening.
  4. Transfer the stud marks from the bottom plate to the top plate with a level held plumb, if you didn't mark them together.

steps.t: Fasten the bottom plate to a wood floor
steps.idea: The bottom plate anchors the wall; fasten into joists where you can.
steps.b:
1. Find the floor joists under the line with a stud finder, or look for nail rows in the subfloor.
  2. Check the plate is exactly on its lines.
  3. Drive two 16d nails or 3" screws at each joist, or every 16" into the subfloor.
  4. {{a.door==='yes'?'Do not fasten inside the door opening; that part gets cut out.':'Fasten within 6" of each end.'}}
  5. Check for pipes, ducts or wires below before you drive anything near them.

steps.t: Fasten the bottom plate to concrete
steps.idea: On concrete, a treated plate on a foam gasket resists moisture; concrete screws hold it down.
steps.b:
1. Lay the sill gasket on the chalk lines under the treated bottom plate.
  2. Drill through the plate and into the concrete with the bit sold with the screws, 1/4" deeper than the screw will go.
  3. Blow or vacuum the dust out of each hole.
  4. Drive about {{c.anchors}} screws: one 6" from each end, {{a.door==='yes'?'one 6" each side of the door opening, ':''}}and about every 24" in between.
  5. Stop when the head is snug. Overdriving strips the concrete.
steps.stop: Radiant heat tubing or a post-tensioned slab (common in some regions; look for a warning stamp in the garage) can be damaged by drilling. Check before drilling. If in doubt, ask a pro.
faq: Can I use a powder-actuated nailer?
Yes. They're fast. Use the right charge strength for your concrete, and wear eye and ear protection. Follow the tool's instructions exactly.

steps.t: Plumb, shim and fasten the top plate
steps.idea: Plumb the wall, shim the gap, then fasten the top plate into every joist or block.
steps.b:
1. Hold the level against the end stud. Push the top until the bubble is centered, then on the edge too.
  2. Line the top plate up with the ceiling chalk line.
  3. At each joist or block, slide a pair of shims into any gap.
  4. {{a.above==='trusses'?'Attach the top plate to each truss with a slotted truss clip, nailed per the clip\'s instructions. Don\'t nail the plate tight to the trusses: they rise and fall with the seasons.':'Drive two 3" screws or 16d nails through the plate and shims into each joist or block.'}}
  5. Check plumb again at both ends and the middle.

steps.t: Toe-nail the studs between the plates
steps.idea: Each stud is cut to fit and nailed at an angle into the plates.
steps.b:
1. Measure between the plates at each X and cut that stud for a snug fit (tap in, not pounded).
  2. Set the stud on its marks, crown facing the same way as the rest.
  3. Drive two 8d nails at about 60 degrees through one face, starting 1" up, into the plate. Then one from the other face.
  4. Do the same at the top.
  5. Check each stud for plumb as you go.
faq: The stud keeps sliding off the mark when I nail.
Screw a scrap block to the plate behind the stud as a stop, or start the nails before you set the stud in place.

steps.t: Frame the door opening in place
steps.idea: Kings first, then jacks, then the header and cripples.
steps.b:
1. Toe-nail the kings to the plates on their marks. Check plumb.
  2. Nail a jack ({{frac(c.jack)}}) to the inside face of each king, every 16".
  3. Set the flat header on the jacks and nail through the kings into its ends.
  4. Toe-nail cripples ({{frac(c.crip)}}) between the header and top plate.
  5. Measure: {{c.ro}}" wide, {{frac(a.roH)}} tall.

steps.t: Tie into the existing wall
steps.idea: The end stud fastens to the old wall top to bottom so it doesn't wobble.
steps.b:
1. Find where the old wall's studs are with a stud finder.
  2. If an old stud lines up with your end stud: drive 3" screws through the end stud into it every 16".
  3. If not: cut a strip of drywall out of the old wall, about 8" wide, floor to ceiling.
  4. Install flat 2x4 blocks between the old studs every 16" to 24" (ladder blocking).
  5. Screw the end stud through the drywall strip area into the blocks, then patch the drywall later.
faq: Can I just use construction adhesive and toggle bolts?
Some people do for a short closet wall, but solid blocking is stronger and gives drywall a corner to fasten to. Use blocking when you can.

steps.t: Cut out the bottom plate in the doorway
steps.idea: Now that the wall is fastened, the plate in the opening can go.
steps.b:
1. Saw the plate flush with the inside face of each jack.
  2. Keep the blade from cutting into the subfloor: angle a handsaw, or use a reciprocating saw blade laid flat.
  3. Pry out the piece.
  4. Re-check the opening width at the bottom, middle and top. It should be the same.

steps.t: Check plumb, straight and square
steps.idea: A quick check now saves fighting the drywall and door later.
steps.b:
1. Hold the level on several studs, both faces. Plumb within about 1/8" over the height.
  2. Stretch a string along the wall face at the top and bottom; studs bowing out more than 1/4" need fixing.
  3. Fix a bowed stud: cut a saw kerf partway into the hollow side, push it straight, and screw a strip across the cut. Or replace it.
  4. {{a.door==='yes'?'Measure the door opening\'s diagonals: they should match within 1/8".':'Measure the wall\'s ends for plumb again.'}}

steps.t: Plan wires, pipes and blocking
steps.idea: Holes for wires and solid wood for shelves or TVs go in before the drywall does.
steps.stop: New outlets and switches usually need a permit and inspection, and in many areas a licensed electrician. Plumbing in the wall usually needs a plumber.
steps.b:
1. Mark where outlets, switches and any shelving or a TV mount will go.
  2. Drill holes through studs in the middle of the stud, no bigger than about 60% of its depth.
  3. Any hole closer than 1-1/4" to the stud face gets a steel nail plate on that face.
  4. Add flat 2x blocking between studs where heavy things will hang.
  5. Take photos with a tape measure in view before drywall goes on.
faq: How big can a hole be?
In a non-bearing wall, codes generally allow up to 60% of the stud depth (about 2" in a 2x4), at least 5/8" from the edge. Check local code.

steps.t: Get the framing inspected
steps.idea: If you have a permit, an inspector checks the framing and any wiring before it's covered.
steps.b:
1. Call for the framing (and electrical rough-in) inspection.
  2. Leave the wall open until it passes.
  3. Fix anything on the correction list and call back.
  4. After it passes: drywall, tape and paint (see the Drywall Repair and Interior Painting guides).

days.wait: Buy lumber; let it sit in the room 1 to 2 days

crownHelp.b:
1. Hold the board by one end at eye level, on edge.
  2. Look down the narrow edge to the far end.
  3. It curves one way a little: the high side is the crown.
  4. Draw an arrow on that side pointing at the crown.
  5. Install all studs with crowns facing the same way.

nailHelp.b:
1. Hold the nail near the tip and tap to start it.
  2. Let go and swing from the elbow with the hammer handle near its end.
  3. Keep the face square to the nail; a glancing blow bends it.
  4. Bent nail? Pull it with the claw and start a new one beside it.
  5. Screws: use 3" structural or construction screws, not drywall screws, which snap.

plumbHelp.b:
1. Hold the level flat against the stud's face, vertical.
  2. Read the end vial (the one across the level's length).
  3. Bubble centered = plumb.
  4. Check the narrow edge too: the wall can lean in two directions.
  5. Flip the level end for end to make sure it reads the same; if not, the level is off.

chalkHelp.b:
1. Hook the line's end on a nail or have a helper hold it on the first mark.
  2. Pull the line tight over the second mark.
  3. Press it to the floor with one hand.
  4. Lift the middle straight up 2" to 3" and let go.
  5. Check the line runs through both marks.

sawHelp.b:
1. Mark the length, then draw a square line with a speed square.
  2. Support the board so the cut-off falls free; never cut between two supports, which pinches the blade.
  3. Line the saw's guide notch up with the waste side of the line.
  4. Let the blade reach full speed, then push steadily.
  5. Keep both hands on the saw and stand to the side of the blade.

plumb.cap: Mark both ends of the wall on the ceiling, then snap a chalk line between the marks.

Mark at 15-1/4",</text><text x="10" y="138">then every 16". Put an X on the far side.</text><text x="10" y="156">Each stud covers 15-1/4" to 16-3/4", so the</text><text x="10" y="168">16", 32", 48" lines fall on stud centers.</text>
layout.cap: Clamp the top and bottom plates together and mark both at once, so the studs line up.

door.svg: <text x="10" y="16" class="k">Door rough opening</text><rect x="60" y="26" width="200" height="6" class="w"/><rect x="60" y="180" width="38" height="8" class="w"/><rect x="222" y="180" width="38" height="8" class="w"/><rect x="110" y="180" width="100" height="8" class="o d"/><rect x="98" y="32" width="6" height="156" class="w"/><rect x="216" y="32" width="6" height="156" class="w"/><rect x="104" y="50" width="6" height="130" class="w"/><rect x="210" y="50" width="6" height="130" class="w"/><rect x="104" y="44" width="112" height="6" class="w"/><rect x="140" y="32" width="6" height="12" class="w"/><rect x="176" y="32" width="6" height="12" class="w"/><line x1="160" y1="110" x2="110" y2="110" class="o"/><polygon points="110,110 114.5,107.8 114.5,112.2" class="inkf"/><line x1="160" y1="110" x2="210" y2="110" class="o"/><polygon points="210,110 205.5,112.2 205.5,107.8" class="inkf"/><text x="160" y="102" class="ac" text-anchor="middle">door width + 2"</text><line x1="240" y1="115" x2="240" y2="50" class="o"/><polygon points="240,50 242.2,54.5 237.8,54.5" class="inkf"/><line x1="240" y1="115" x2="240" y2="180" class="o"/><polygon points="240,180 237.8,175.5 242.2,175.5" class="inkf"/><text x="246" y="112" class="ac">82-1/2"</text><text x="246" y="124">typical</text><text x="10" y="92" class="k">king</text><line x1="34" y1="89" x2="98" y2="89" class="a"/><text x="10" y="140" class="k">jack</text><line x1="34" y1="137" x2="104" y2="137" class="a"/><text x="10" y="52" class="k">header</text><line x1="48" y1="49" x2="104" y2="47" class="a"/><text x="160" y="206" text-anchor="middle">Check the size your door's instructions give.</text>
door.cap: An 80" prehung door usually needs 82-1/2" from the subfloor to the header. Width is the door slab plus 2".

tilt.svg: <text x="10" y="16" class="k">Build it short enough to tilt up</text><line x1="10" y1="26" x2="310" y2="26" class="o" style="stroke-width:3"/><rect x="10" y="176" width="300" height="6" class="w"/><path d="M46 72 A147 147 0 0 1 150 29" class="a d" fill="none"/><g><rect x="150" y="30" width="10" height="146" class="w"/><animateTransform attributeName="transform" type="rotate" values="-70 150 176;0 150 176;0 150 176" keyTimes="0;0.6;1" dur="3.5s" repeatCount="indefinite"/></g><text x="176" y="46" class="k">diagonal must clear</text><text x="176" y="58">the ceiling</text><text x="176" y="96" class="ac">build the wall 1/2"</text><text x="176" y="108">shorter than the</text><text x="176" y="120">ceiling, then shim</text><text x="20" y="196">Lift with a helper. Keep the bottom plate on its line.</text>
tilt.title: Tilt the wall up
tilt.cap: The corner-to-corner measurement of the wall is a bit longer than its height, so a full-height wall jams as it swings up.

toenail.svg: <text x="10" y="16" class="k">Toe-nail at about 60 degrees</text><rect x="30" y="140" width="260" height="18" class="w"/><rect x="140" y="30" width="30" height="110" class="w"/><g><line x1="132" y1="107" x2="154" y2="146" class="o" style="stroke-width:3"/><line x1="127" y1="110" x2="137" y2="104" class="o" style="stroke-width:3"/><animateTransform attributeName="transform" type="translate" values="-14 -24;0 0;0 0" keyTimes="0;0.5;1" dur="2.6s" repeatCount="indefinite"/></g><line x1="178" y1="107" x2="156" y2="146" class="o" style="stroke-width:3"/><line x1="173" y1="104" x2="183" y2="110" class="o" style="stroke-width:3"/><text x="10" y="96" class="k">start about 1"</text><text x="10" y="108">up the stud</text><text x="196" y="96" class="k">one more from</text><text x="196" y="108">the other side</text><text x="30" y="176">plate</text><text x="176" y="40">stud</text><text x="10" y="194">Two or three per side. A block behind the stud</text><text x="10" y="206">keeps it from sliding off its mark.</text>
toenail.title: Drive a toe-nail
toenail.cap: The nail goes through the stud and into the plate at an angle. 8d nails or 3" screws both work.

shims.svg: <text x="10" y="16" class="k">Shim gaps at the top plate</text><rect x="10" y="26" width="300" height="20" class="w"/><rect x="10" y="46" width="300" height="6" class="b"/><rect x="10" y="64" width="300" height="16" class="w"/><polygon points="110,52 210,52 210,64" class="y"/><polygon points="110,52 110,64 210,64" class="y" style="opacity:.7"/><rect x="158" y="34" width="4" height="50" class="inkf"/><rect x="152" y="80" width="16" height="4" class="inkf"/><text x="14" y="40" class="k">joist</text><text x="14" y="76" class="k">top plate</text><text x="10" y="118" class="k">1 Slide a pair of shims in, one from each side.</text><text x="10" y="132">2 Tap them until snug, not tight.</text><text x="10" y="146">3 Fasten through the shims into the joist.</text><text x="10" y="160">4 Snap off the extra.</text>
shims.cap: Without shims, a screw pulls the plate up into a bow and the wall goes out of plumb.

intersect.svg: <text x="10" y="16" class="k">Where the new wall meets an old one</text><rect x="10" y="30" width="140" height="120" class="b"/><rect x="14" y="30" width="8" height="120" class="w"/><rect x="138" y="30" width="8" height="120" class="w"/><rect x="22" y="44" width="116" height="6" class="w"/><rect x="22" y="76" width="116" height="6" class="w"/><rect x="22" y="108" width="116" height="6" class="w"/><rect x="22" y="138" width="116" height="6" class="w"/><rect x="66" y="30" width="28" height="120" class="mos" style="opacity:.6"/><text x="10" y="166" class="k">Ladder blocking</text><text x="10" y="178">flat 2x4s every 16" to 24"</text><rect x="170" y="60" width="140" height="14" class="b"/><rect x="226" y="40" width="26" height="20" class="w"/><rect x="226" y="74" width="26" height="70" class="mos"/><rect x="232" y="74" width="14" height="10" class="w"/><text x="170" y="34" class="k">existing stud</text><text x="260" y="120">new</text><text x="260" y="132">wall</text><text x="170" y="166" class="k">Or land on a stud</text><text x="170" y="178">top view: screw into it</text>
intersect.cap: The new wall's end stud needs solid wood behind the old drywall to screw into, top to bottom.

nailplate.svg: <text x="10" y="16" class="k">Protect wires with a nail plate</text><rect x="100" y="70" width="120" height="50" class="w"/><circle cx="160" cy="95" r="20" class="bk"/><circle cx="160" cy="95" r="5" class="y"/><rect x="94" y="64" width="6" height="62" class="tb"/><rect x="220" y="64" width="6" height="62" class="tb"/><line x1="30" y1="95" x2="90" y2="95" class="bad"/><polygon points="90,95 84.6,97.6 84.6,92.4" class="badf"/><line x1="120" y1="140" x2="100" y2="140" class="o"/><polygon points="100,140 104.5,137.8 104.5,142.2" class="inkf"/><line x1="120" y1="140" x2="140" y2="140" class="o"/><polygon points="140,140 135.5,142.2 135.5,137.8" class="inkf"/><text x="10" y="84" class="k">drywall</text><text x="10" y="112" class="k">screw</text><text x="120" y="156" class="ac">under 1-1/4": add plates</text><text x="100" y="50" class="k">steel plate on each face</text><text x="160" y="36" text-anchor="middle">stud seen from above (cut)</text><text x="10" y="180">Center holes. Max about 60% of the stud depth.</text>
nailplate.cap: A drywall screw can't reach a wire or pipe behind a steel plate.

glossary: A wall that divides space and carries no load from above.
A wall that holds up joists, rafters or a floor above. Never change one without an engineer.
The horizontal 2x4s at the bottom (sole plate) and top of a wall.
Measured from the center of one stud to the center of the next.
The framed hole a door or window fits into, a bit bigger than the unit.
A full-height stud on each side of an opening.
A shorter stud nailed to the king that holds up the header.
The horizontal piece over an opening.
A short stud above a header or below a window.
Short pieces of lumber between joists or studs for fastening or support.
A nail driven at an angle through the side of one board into another.
The slight upward curve along a board's edge.
A factory-built triangle frame that supports a roof; moves slightly with the seasons.
A window big enough and low enough to escape through in a fire.
